claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast eutectic CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a well-defined multiphase microstructure containing phase boundaries.
At elevated temperature under wear, thermally activated diffusion causes chromium to move away from phase boundaries.
Chromium diffusion produces chromium-depleted regions at phase boundaries.
Chromium depletion at phase boundaries compromises local passive-film formation or stability.
Compromised passive films increase localized anodic dissolution at wear tracks.
Controlled chromium doping can selectively enrich particular phases and phase boundaries without altering the overall eutectic structure.
Chromium enrichment at phase boundaries reinforces passive-film formation.
Enhanced local chromium concentration preserves passive-film integrity during mechanical disruption.
Preservation of the passive film reduces localized corrosion under wear conditions.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the chromium-enhanced alloy will have lower total degradation and mass loss.
Relative to the baseline, the chromium-enhanced alloy will have a lower and steadier corrosion rate.
The abrasion component of wear will be similar in the chromium-enhanced and undoped alloys.
Chromium enrichment will significantly reduce corrosion-related pitting and repassivation cycling.
The proposed mechanism is active during sustained exposure at 350–450 °C in an aggressive chloride-rich environment with adequate mechanical loading.
If thermal and mechanical energy are insufficient to drive significant chromium diffusion, chromium depletion will not be the dominant degradation pathway.
